newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: PACKAGED TOURS BRING IN BILLIONS
Packaged tours for overseas visitors have made Australian tour operators almost one and a half billion dollars over the past year.
Most of the tours were bought by Japanese holidaymakers who paid an average of A$1,110 compared to Americans who paid about A$970.
Between June 1995 and 96, one point six million overseas visitors travelled to Australia on packaged tours bought from Australian based inbound tour operators.
Forty-two percent came from Japan, 33 percent from other Asian nations, eight percent from Europe, and six per cent from North America and the UK, and Ireland.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics survey found the local inbound tour market employs three thousand 740 people in Australia and 410 staff abroad.
ESTIMATED 10,000 SUBMISSIONS TO EUTHANASIA INQUIRY
An estimated 10,000 submissions have been received by a Senate Committee inquiry into the Northern Territory's voluntary euthanasia law.
Territory Senator Grant Tambling says that's the highest number of submissions ever received by a Parliamentary Committee, indicating it's an issue close to the hearts of many Australians.
Senator Tambling says despite the passing of the Kevin Andrews anti-euthanasia bill by the House of Representatives, there's a good chance the Senate will overturn it.
PORT LINCOLN WARNED ABOUT POSSIBLE RACIST TAG
The people of Port Lincoln in South Australia are being urged to rally against racism, or face the possibility of hurting the town's export tuna market.
South Australian Federal Liberal MP Chris Gallus says results of the weekend Council by-election could see the town labelled as racist.
Supporters of Mayor Peter Davis were elected in all five wards, with only four of the nine councillors who resigned over his controversial comments against multicuturalism, regaining their seats.
Ms Gallus says Port Lincoln residents should get together and issue a statement supporting multiculturalism and rejecting racism to avoid any adverse publicity or threats to the export market.
D-DAY FOR BHP WORKERS
Union delegates at BHP's Port Kembla and Newcastle steelworks will today decide whether to accept a pay deal for BHP workers negotiated in the New South Wales Industrial Commission last week.
The pay offer, believed to be 10 per cent, was aimed at averting a national steel industry strike last Friday.
BHP had offered its workers 8.5 percent while the unions' were seeking 15 percent.
PORT HINCHINBROOK RESORT UNDER SPOTLIGHT
A federal court appeal gets underway in Sydney today against Federal Government approval for Keith Williams' Port Hinchinbrook Resort development in North Queensland.
Further speculation on the development's future has been raised following reports it includes a residential area.
The North Queensland Conservation Council's David Haigh is calling on Environment Minister Robert Hill to rule out such a development because there's been no consent for it.
Keith Williams says the residential area has been in the plans from day one.
But Mr Haige says a real estate development would be against the World Heritage Convention, against planning permission, and against the local govenment Act of Queensland.
ALP HAPPY DESPITE LOSS IN WA POLL
Despite its defeat in Saturday's state election, the West Australian Labor Party is feeling confident and relaxed about spending four more years in Opposition.
The predicted loss of up to nine ALP seats didn't eventuate, with Labor gaining a slight swing at the poll but not enough to depose the Court government.
Labor leader Geoff Gallop, whose own seat was in doubt prior to the poll, is describing the vote as a positive result.
He says the Labor Party in West Australia is on the way up after gaining its first ground since 1983.
But returned Premier Richard Court has laughed off Labor's interpretation of the result, saying there's little to justify the ALP's satisfaction.
ULTRA-MARATHON RUNNER TAKES IT EASY
The new world record holder for running non-stop across the Simpson Desert will begin his recovery process this morning.

Pat Farmer arrived in Birdsville at about 20 to midnight, Queensland time, last night, some 21 minutes inside the previous record of three days-17 hours-52 minutes and 18 seconds for the 379 kilometre marathon.
He headed straight to a specially transported spa bath, where he was greeted by his family and a band of supporters.
One of the attempt's sponsors Larry Shutes says despite the ordeal, Farmer was in a surprisingly good condition.
